title: Litex SoC binds to non-existent ports when generating a NaxRiscv-based SoC with --with-jtag-instruction
body:
Hello,

# Issue
I'm trying to implement a NaxRiscv-based SoC on FPGA (Digilent Genesys 2) but synthesis fails, as the SoC's top level module instantiating the Nax tries to connect to port which do not exist.

Precisely, I'm trying to add a JTAG debug module within the Nax, which thus exposes I/O ports in the Nax's top level. For some reason, when integrating the Nax in the SoC's top level, Litex seems to detect different signal names for the JTAG ports, than the ones actually exposed by the Nax, which thus causes an error during synthesis.


Instantation of the NaxRiscv in the SoC top module (namely the verilog file ```build/gateware/digilent_genesys2.v```)
```verilog
//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Instance NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934 of NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934 Module.
//------------------------------------------------------------------------------
NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934 NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934(
        /* Remaining ports connections */
        .jtag_instruction_capture           (basesoc_jtag_capture),
        .jtag_instruction_clk               (basesoc_jtag_clk),
        .jtag_instruction_enable            (basesoc_jtag_enable),
        .jtag_instruction_reset             (basesoc_jtag_reset),
        .jtag_instruction_shift             (basesoc_jtag_shift),
        .jtag_instruction_tdi               (basesoc_jtag_tdi),
        .jtag_instruction_update            (basesoc_jtag_update),
        /* Remaining ports connections */
       	);
```

Definition of the NaxRiscv top module
```verilog
module NaxRiscvLitex_ac66cf5e80a0da4a2f58fc5f9f240934 (
	/* Remaining ports declaration */
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_tdi,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_enable,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_capture,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_shift,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_update,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_reset,
	output wire          jtag_instruction_instruction_tdo,
	input  wire          jtag_instruction_clk
	/* Remaining ports declaration */
);
	/* RTL */
endmodule
```

As one can see from the above RTL snippets, except for ```jtag_instruction_clk``` which is correct, JTAG signals are declared with prefix ```jtag_instruction_instruction``` whilst the SoC is mapping to ports with prefix ```jtag_instruction```.

# Build options

Here are my build options to try and recreate the issue :
```bash
python3 -m litex_boards.targets.digilent_genesys2.py \
--cpu-type=naxriscv \
--toolchain=vivado \
--build \
--bios-console=lite --bios-format=double \
--synth-mode=vivado \
--bus-standard=wishbone --bus-data-width=32 --bus-address-width=32 --bus-interconnect=crossbar \
--watchdog-width=32 \
--uart-name=serial --uart-baudrate=921600 --uart-fifo-depth=16 \
--l2-size=1024 --integrated-rom-size=131072 --integrated-sram-size=16536 --integrated-main-ram-size=0 \
--sys-clk-freq=200000000.0 \
--no-netlist-cache --update-repo=latest \
--cpu-variant=standard --xlen=32 --cpu-count=1 \
--l2-bytes=131072 --l2-ways=8 --with-rvc --with-fpu --with-coherent-dma \
--with-jtag-instruction
```

Actually, I use a modified version of ```litex_boards.targets.digilent_genesys2``` in which I added  the following lines (right-after the ```BaseSoc``` instantiation in ```main()```) :

```python
from litex.soc.cores.jtag import XilinxJTAG
soc.jtag = jtag = XilinxJTAG(XilinxJTAG.get_primitive(soc.platform.device), chain=4)
soc.comb += [
    soc.cpu.jtag_reset.eq(jtag.reset),
    soc.cpu.jtag_capture.eq(jtag.capture),
    soc.cpu.jtag_shift.eq(jtag.shift),
    soc.cpu.jtag_update.eq(jtag.update),
    soc.cpu.jtag_clk.eq(jtag.tck),
    soc.cpu.jtag_tdi.eq(jtag.tdi),
    soc.cpu.jtag_enable.eq(True),
    jtag.tdo.eq(soc.cpu.jtag_tdo),
]
```

Note: I added the latter modifications following this tutorial from Litex Wiki [JTAG GDB Debugging with VexRiscv SMP NaxRiscv VexiiRiscv CPUs](https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/wiki/JTAG-GDB-Debugging-with-VexRiscv-SMP-NaxRiscv-VexiiRiscv-CPUs#debugging-on-physical-hardware-directly-though-bscane2-jtag-primitive), as I would like to route the JTAG module to the FPGA's built-in JTAG.

# Question

I was wondering if anyone knows why Litex catches wrong names specifically for these signals ? Also, perhaps, is there a way to force the name of these ```XilinxJTAG``` signals to have prefix ```jtag_instruction``` instead of ```jtag_instruction_instruction``` ?

Thanks,
Regards,

comments.body:
Hello @benjaminh-13,

I suggest 2 solutions: 

- either make a modification on the NaxRiscv side, 
- or make a modification on the Litex side.

#### On the NaxRiscv side

You'll need to modify the file that generates the SoC for Litex, NaxSoc, by changing this line :

https://github.com/SpinalHDL/NaxRiscv/blob/43716b5770e8ac689e9778056c061da577dcf17e/src/main/scala/naxriscv/platform/litex/NaxSoc.scala#L209

by this one : 

```scala
if (withJtagInstruction) debug.instruction.setName("jtag")
```

What happens is that the string `jtag_instruction` is added to the variable name `instruction` in [DebugModuleFiber](https://github.com/SpinalHDL/SpinalHDL/blob/af8fab4da5a73c785c4f2e2f68af2c9b34fd6aec/lib/src/main/scala/spinal/lib/cpu/riscv/debug/DebugModuleFiber.scala#L95) when the verilog is generated.

So to change the name of the totality, another way would be as follows :

```scala
if (withJtagInstruction) debug.instruction.instruction.setName("jtag_instruction")
```

#### On the Litex side

You need to modify the core.py file associated with NaxRiscv.

https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/blob/48e65c199de6bd1d5aead61d7f515356cc7ecab8/litex/soc/cores/cpu/naxriscv/core.py#L428-L437

You need to update the assignments with the “jtag_instruction_instruction” prefix.

```python
self.cpu_params.update(
    i_jtag_instruction_clk     = self.jtag_clk,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_enable  = self.jtag_enable,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_capture = self.jtag_capture,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_shift   = self.jtag_shift,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_update  = self.jtag_update,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_reset   = self.jtag_reset,
    i_jtag_instruction_instruction_tdi     = self.jtag_tdi,
    o_jtag_instruction_instruction_tdo     = self.jtag_tdo,
)
```

After one of these two modifications, the Vivado synthesis should work.

Best regards

Hello @atkarim,

Thank you for the very quick response.

I tried solution 2, namely bringing changes to the NaxRiscv's ```core.py``` in Litex and now synthesis succeeds. As a consequence, I am closing this issue.

Thanks again,
Best regards,

title: Quick start guide (for advanced users) - RISC-V toolchain not detected
body:
Following the quick start for advanced users, the RISC-V toolchain is not detected as I get the following error:
OSError: Unable to find any of the cross compilation toolchains:
- riscv64-unknown-elf
- riscv32-unknown-elf
- riscv-none-embed

In other words, `litex/litex/soc/integration/export.py` returns `None` when it tries `which("riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc")`

Strange thing, the RISC-V toolchain is in my PATH...
`pascal@laptop:$ riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc

riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc: fatal error: no input files`

I'll investigate this issue a bit later.

comments.body:
Thanks for reporting, are you using a specific OS?

Do you have the same results if you run the following commands in the python3 shell?:
````
>>> from shutil import which
>>> which("riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc")
'/opt/riscv/bin/riscv64-unknown-elf-gcc'
>>> 
````
Yes, that's the thing I've tried afterwards :/

I've found my mistake:
- Running `litex_setup.py init install` as a normal user. Doesn't work as it it wants to write stuff is `usr/local/lib`.
- Running `litex_setup.py init install` as sudo.
- Running the next steps as written in the `readme`.

Things would have worked better if I ran `./litex_setup.py init install --user` (my bad...)

In my current setup, I had to `chown` my `enjoy-digital` directory (where `litex_setup.py` was downloaded) to myself before it works :100:

Just to give more clarity , what I am doing is writing a 32bit value to a `uint32_t` variable in the C code and set its address to the DMA to read and transfer to a CSR status register which I am then reading and printing in the C code, where the mismatch is observed.

I re-checked the current code and your observation still makes sense for a direct word-level use of `WishboneDMAReader`.

For a little-endian CPU writing `0xcafef00d` as a `uint32_t`, the Wishbone word read back by the DMA is already `0xcafef00d`. Passing `endianness="little"` to `WishboneDMAReader` then applies `reverse_bytes()`, so a direct word consumer such as a CSR status register will see `0x0df0feca`.

So for raw word-oriented use, the DMA should be instantiated with `endianness="big"` / no byte swap.

I would avoid flipping the global `format_bytes()` mapping since the DMA is also used in byte-stream storage paths, where this conversion is part of the expected byte ordering. The real issue is that the parameter is confusing for direct word users, so we should probably document this better and/or add a clearer no-swap/raw mode in the future.

This has now been improved with:  c4baeb3e1a3a35ecaa3e47eae4d2951b64d76bdd

The existing DMA endianness behavior is kept for compatibility: `endianness="little"` still byte-swaps and `endianness="big"` still preserves the raw Wishbone word.

To make direct word-oriented use cases clearer, `WishboneDMAReader` and `WishboneDMAWriter` now also have an explicit `with_byteswap` override. So for a raw word transfer such as the `0xcafef00d` case discussed here, the DMA can now be instantiated with:

```python
  WishboneDMAReader(bus, endianness="little", with_byteswap=False)
```

This preserves the raw Wishbone word instead of byte-swapping it.

I also added regression coverage for the reported word-level case on both reader and writer, checking both the legacy little-endian byte-swap behavior and the explicit no-swap path.

I also added a follow-up test commit to double-check the default behavior: https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/commit/db2678d1a2df8f47c76510fec134c4a093cf45cc

This adds regression coverage for the storage-style byte-stream path used by LiteSDCard/LiteSATA, where DMA words are converted to/from 8-bit streams with reverse stream converters.

The tests confirm why the legacy default remains unchanged for these users, while raw word-oriented users can use the explicit `with_byteswap=False` override added above.

With the explicit `with_byteswap=False` override and the added regression tests for both raw word and byte-stream DMA paths, I think this is now covered. Closing, but please reopen or open a follow-up if another DMA endianness case still behaves unexpectedly.

def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="LiteX SoC on Arty A7")
    parser.add_argument("--toolchain",           default="vivado",                 help="Toolchain use to build (default: vivado)")
    parser.add_argument("--build",               action="store_true",              help="Build bitstream")
    parser.add_argument("--load",                action="store_true",              help="Load bitstream")
    parser.add_argument("--variant",             default="a7-35",                  help="Board variant: a7-35 (default) or a7-100")
    parser.add_argument("--sys-clk-freq",        default=100e6,                    help="System clock frequency (default: 100MHz)")
    ethopts = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group()
    ethopts.add_argument("--with-ethernet",      action="store_true",              help="Enable Ethernet support")
    ethopts.add_argument("--with-etherbone",     action="store_true",              help="Enable Etherbone support")
    parser.add_argument("--eth-ip",              default="192.168.1.50", type=str, help="Ethernet/Etherbone IP address")
    parser.add_argument("--eth-dynamic-ip",      action="store_true",              help="Enable dynamic Ethernet IP addresses setting")
    sdopts = parser.add_mutually_exclusive_group()
    sdopts.add_argument("--with-spi-sdcard",     action="store_true",              help="Enable SPI-mode SDCard support")
    sdopts.add_argument("--with-sdcard",         action="store_true",              help="Enable SDCard support")
    parser.add_argument("--sdcard-adapter",      type=str,                         help="SDCard PMOD adapter: digilent (default) or numato")
    parser.add_argument("--with-jtagbone",       action="store_true",              help="Enable Jtagbone support")
    parser.add_argument("--with-mapped-flash",   action="store_true",              help="Enable Memory Mapped Flash")
    parser.add_argument("--with-spi-flash",      action="store_true",              help="Enable SPI Flash (MMAPed)")
    parser.add_argument("--with-pmod-gpio",      action="store_true",              help="Enable GPIOs through PMOD") # FIXME: Temporary test.
    builder_args(parser)
    soc_core_args(parser)
    vivado_build_args(parser)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    assert not (args.with_etherbone and args.eth_dynamic_ip)

    soc = BaseSoC(
        variant        = args.variant,
        toolchain      = args.toolchain,
        sys_clk_freq   = int(float(args.sys_clk_freq)),
        with_ethernet  = args.with_ethernet,
        with_etherbone = args.with_etherbone,
        eth_ip         = args.eth_ip,
        eth_dynamic_ip = args.eth_dynamic_ip,
        with_jtagbone  = args.with_jtagbone,
        with_mapped_flash = args.with_mapped_flash,
        with_spi_flash = args.with_spi_flash,
        with_pmod_gpio = args.with_pmod_gpio,
        **soc_core_argdict(args)

    if args.with_spi_sdcard:
        soc.add_spi_sdcard()
    if args.with_sdcard:
        soc.add_sdcard()
    builder = Builder(soc, **builder_argdict(args))
    builder_kwargs = vivado_build_argdict(args) if args.toolchain == "vivado" else {}
    builder.build(**builder_kwargs, run=args.build)

        prog = soc.platform.create_programmer()
        prog.load_bitstream(os.path.join(builder.gateware_dir, soc.build_name + ".bit"))

if __name__ == "__main__":

title: microwatt BIOS hangs in ISR
body:
With the current LiteX versions and the Microwatt CPU (`--cpu-type=microwatt --cpu-variant=standard+ghdl+irq`) the BIOS hangs in the ISR with what appears to be a wild jump to an invalid address outside of the memory space.  This in turn results in no console output and is repeatable in simulation.

I've attached a simulation trace database and the BIOS files generated from a Debian Bullseye ppc64le host system for analysis.  The last instructions executed appear to be as follows:

```
        /* Load IRQ handler address from SRAM */
        LOAD_IMM64(%r3, __isr_address)
    102c:       00 00 60 3c     lis     r3,0
    1030:       00 00 63 60     ori     r3,r3,0
    1034:       c6 07 63 78     rldicr  r3,r3,32,31
    1038:       00 00 63 64     oris    r3,r3,0
    103c:       00 00 63 60     ori     r3,r3,0
        ld      %r3,   0(%r3)
    1040:       00 00 63 e8     ld      r3,0(r3)

        mtctr   %r3,
    1044:       a6 03 69 7c     mtctr   r3
        mr      %r3, %r10
    1048:       78 53 43 7d     mr      r3,r10
        bctrl
    104c:       21 04 80 4e     bctrl

<jump to invalid address 0x4800002408000048>
```
[simulation_output_and_bios_files.zip](https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/files/8399156/simulation_output_and_bios_files.zip)

comments.body: May be related to #1077
@shenki Any chance you might be able to take a look at this?

From what I can tell, objdump might be mistranslating `bctrl`, microwatt is processing that instruction as a `bcctr` (not sure which is correct right now, so I'm assuming microwatt is doing the right thing).

If true, the invalid jump is caused by `ld      r3,0(r3)` loading the data at 0x0 into r3, which is obviously incorrect.  Starting to suspect `__isr_address` might be wrong at this point.

Confirmed, `LOAD_IMM64(%r3, __isr_address)` is loading 0x0 (ROM base) instead of the correct location 0x100000 (SRAM base).

When run without IRQ support the console does come up, but there are residual issues that may be caused by related linking errors.  Will continue to debug here.

OK, it appears this has been an issue for quite a while and no one was testing, including on our side, as we were using a different boot firmware that takes advantage of the `SPR_KAISB` feature.

I'll be spending some time to apply https://gitlab.raptorengineering.com/kestrel-collaboration/kestrel-firmware/bootrom/-/merge_requests/10 to the LiteX tree and creating a new pull request once I know it's working...

Thanks @madscientist159, it's planned to add Microwatt testing to the CI (at it is currently done for most supported RISC-V CPUs), but this hasn't been done yet but we could put more efforts into this.

This should now be covered by current LiteX.

I also tested the Microwatt IRQ boot path locally with both:

  - `--cpu-variant=standard+irq`
  - `--cpu-variant=standard+ghdl+irq`

Both reached the LiteX BIOS prompt, so I can no longer reproduce the original ISR hang.

CI has also been updated with enjoy-digital/litex@de10ffc154a66c1798943f3070101d2825611061 so `test_cpu[microwatt]` now exercises the `standard+irq` variant directly.

I think this can now be closed. If an IRQ-specific Microwatt boot issue still reproduces on current LiteX, please open a fresh issue with the updated reproducer.

title: liblitedram accessors change causes build failure on ecp5 boards
body:
Some combination of commit 58fda1a3 ("liblitedram: Move PHY accessors to a separate file") and/or commit 4c605020 ("liblitedram: Codebase cleanup") result in a failure to build on ecp5 boards (tested on trellisboard and ecpix5):

```
riscv64-unknown-elf/bin/ld: ../liblitedram/liblitedram.a(accessors.o): in function `write_inc_dq_bitslip':
/litex/litex/soc/software/liblitedram/accessors.c:116: undefined reference to `ddrphy_wdly_dq_bitslip_write'
riscv64-unknown-elf/12.2.0/../../../../riscv64-unknown-elf/bin/ld: ../liblitedram/liblitedram.a(accessors.o): in function `write_rst_dq_bitslip':
/litex/litex/soc/software/liblitedram/accessors.c:122: undefined reference to `ddrphy_wdly_dq_bitslip_rst_write'
collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
```

From a cursory analysis it appears that the new conditional:

```
+#if defined(SDRAM_PHY_BITSLIPS)
```

doesn't adequately cover the conditions existent on ecp5 boards, whereas the old one:

```
-#if defined(SDRAM_PHY_WRITE_LATENCY_CALIBRATION_CAPABLE) || defined(SDRAM_BITSLIP_CAPABLE)
```

did. Test/debug using the following command line:

```
litex-boards/litex_boards/targets/lambdaconcept_ecpix5.py --build --cpu-type vexriscv
```

The cpu type doesn't really matter, it's the conditional compilation of accessors depending on register accessors generated in `build/lambdaconcept_ecpix5/software/include/generated/csr.h` that appears to be the problem.

@mtdudek @michalsieron @enjoy-digital -- can you double-check the `#ifdef` magic changes acrosss these commits? Thanks!

- YosysWrapper can optionally route SystemVerilog sources through read_slang, while keeping read_verilog -sv as the default.

fix_commits.messageHeadline: build/sim: define default Verilator user hooks

comments.body:
Thanks for the detailed log. The failure appears to come from the optional Verilator user hooks used by the LiteX simulator:

```
litex_sim_user_init
litex_sim_user_pre_eval
litex_sim_user_post_eval
```

These were declared as undefined weak symbols so user code could optionally provide them. That can still leave unresolved symbols at final link on Darwin/arm64 when no user hook source is provided, which matches the linker error in your log.

I opened a fix here:
https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/pull/2509

The PR provides weak no-op default definitions for these hooks, while still allowing user-provided strong definitions through `--verilator-extra-source` to override them.

Tested with:

```
python3 -m py_compile litex/build/sim/verilator.py test/build/test_sim_verilator.py
pytest -q test/build/test_sim_verilator.py
```
Thanks, also working on my side.

```

The second run of ecppack, without the --spimode flag, produces a bitstream which can be programmed. The first run is consistently broken.

fix_commits.messageHeadline: build/lattice/trellis: set default spimode to None (--spimode not pas…

comments.body:
Ecppack puts "0x79 0x49 0x00 0x00" into the bitstream when --spimode fast-read is set.  dual-spi spimode adds "0x79 0x51 0x00 0x00" and qspi adds "0x79 0x59 0x00 0x00".

When the --spimode flag is omitted then this sequence is omitted completely.

My 5A-75E flash chip doesn't like any of the above spimode options so I would need to be able to omit the spimode flag. Perhaps it could default to nothing instead of fast-read. It begins to look like it isn't really an ecppack issue after all.

OK, a last comment. If I use

`openFPGALoader -c ft2232 -f top.bit`

to write the bitstream to flash then the bitstream produced by --spimode fast-read works! My flash chip does like the fast-read mode after all.

I guess the bottom line is that bitstreams created with spimode options cannot be used for SRAM uploads.

Yes, that is correct, the SPI mode flags break uploads via JTAG or other SRAM programming routes. prjtrellis actually strips them automagically when creating an svf file, but that doesn't help when creating a bit file for another programming tool.

Thanks @derekmulcahy, @daveshah1, with https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/commit/6671eb6218ce35a4b79f3c6dbbb2092bcaa3b41f spimode is set to None by default (and --spimode is not passed to ecppack in this case).
Awesome! Fixed while I slept!

title: Zynq address decoding issue
body:
While working on a target using Zynq7000 cpu I stumbled upon a problem with decoding the address space / selecting suitable bus to perform operation on CSRs.
I’m trying to add a single non-LiteX peripheral to a Zynq7000 SoC, behind AXI2Wishbone bridge of base address `0x43c0 0000`. The peripheral is connected via wishbone bus that follows to the core’s decoder, where the control is delegated further. It also provides two AXI slaves and these are too connected in the target but they’re not the focus of the problem.
From what I’ve been able to trace back there were some changes made regarding the `csr_decode` property in Zynq7000 with commit [f46d1c1](https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/commit/f46d1c190b9dc87ecfea43def69862ce99d99559). And I do understand it was introduced in order to be able to decode the addresses correctly while using the bridge, however, disabling the decoding SoCRegion in Zynq7000 seems to cause an issue where the `csr_bridge` the LiteX is placing (while finalizing the SoC) is always selected. Therefore, always being granted access to the data channel. I.e. rdata for Zynq7000.

```
always @(*) begin                          	 
	slave_sel <= 2'd0;                     	 
	slave_sel[0] <= (shared_adr[29:15] == 1'd0);
	slave_sel[1] <= 1'd1;                  	 
end 
```
                                       	 
Where then `slave_sel` is assigned to `slave_sel_r`.
```
always @(*) begin                                                                                            	 
	(..)
	shared_dat_r <= (({32{slave_sel_r[0]}} & wb_control_dat_r) | ({32{slave_sel_r[1]}} & basesoc_wishbone_dat_r));
```

Where `wb_control_dat_r` is assigned to my core’s `dat_o` and the `basesoc_wishbone_dat_r` is from various data sources generated by LiteX infrastructure.
When simply enabling default decoding in `Zynq7000` cpu in target:
```
self.cpu.csr_decode = True
```
The generated verilog changes to:
```
always @(*) begin                               	 
	slave_sel <= 2'd0;                          	 
	slave_sel[0] <= (shared_adr[29:15] == 1'd0);	 
	slave_sel[1] <= (shared_adr[29:14] == 15'd17344);
end                       
```                      	 
(the rest stays the same)
In which case, the data passed by my core doesn’t get or’ed with the data passed from base soc.
Now, the way I constructed my target is I placed the bridge at `0x43c0 0000` and I placed my core at the `SoCRegion` of origin 0x0, this way it’s address is properly decoded even if zynq's  `csr_decode = True`.
I don’t know why exactly changing the decoding in zynq impacts the selection this greatly. Looks like it got optimised this way.

# Disable Misaligned

title: soc/software/bios: The linker script breaks linkage with `--build-id` flag
body:
After running LiteDRAM's `test_examples.py` tests it turned out there's a linkage problem when GCC is configured with `--enable-linker-build-id` which makes it pass the `--build-id` flag to a linker. Using that option with current BIOS linker scripts ends up in such an error:
```
  <PATH>/ld.bfd.real: section .note.gnu.build-id LMA [0000000000000000,0000000000000023] overlaps section .text LMA [0000000000000000,0000000000005333]
  collect2: error: ld returned 1 exit status
  make: *** [<PATH>/litex/soc/software/bios/Makefile:60: bios.elf] Error 1
```

fix_commits.messageHeadline: bios: mark .note.gnu.build-id as non-loadable but don't disable it

comments.body: CC @danc86
@shenki - You were doing something here right?
Might be related to https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/pull/1020 ?

The testing was indeed conducted with an older LiteX revision (https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/commit/ab9f214a5ee4ab5bf96e19ff3520cf59092ad11a) so there should be no such error after that change. Passing `--build-id=none` prohibits a linker from adding the `build-id`.

Sorry for not testing the latest revision before creating this issue. I'll let you know after I check if this change is enough.
As expected, the BIOS is buildable after making such a change in `common.mak`. Still, I'll leave closing the issue to @danc86 as he might want to add something to it.

Thanks @ajelinski.

I don't think overriding `--build-id` to turn it off is the best approach, if the environment has explicitly requested it. Distros like Chrome OS generally want to inject a build id and expect that the resulting ELF executable will have the `.note.gnu.build-id` section, so that their debuginfo processing can do stuff with it.

More generally, non-loadable `.note` sections are used for injecting various other kinds of metadata into the executable, like Fedora's [annobin plugin](https://developers.redhat.com/blog/2018/02/20/annobin-storing-information-binaries#how_to_use_it). And DWARF debug sections fall into this category too, they are extra metadata kept in the ELF output even though they will not be included in the final firmware image.

The issue with `--build-id` seems to just be that the `.note.gnu.build-id` section is marked *loadable*, unlike the other kinds of metadata sections. As far as I can tell, this is done so that programs can extract their own build id at runtime. I even found [a blog post](https://interrupt.memfault.com/blog/gnu-build-id-for-firmware) about using it in embedded firmware to identify the version of code running, which is an interesting idea.

But since the Litex BIOS can't use the build id at runtime I would suggest to just mark it non-loadable in the linker script, so that it's kept in the ELF but doesn't cause an error by overlapping with .text and won't be copied to the final `bios.bin` image. I've sent PR #1044 for that.

Either way, the issue with `--build-id` doesn't happen with the latest `master` branch so we can definitely close this issue.
@shenki - Thoughts?
I'm closing the issue since the problem is fixed and the change proposed by @danc86 has its own PR where it can be discussed.

Hello, it seems that I've managed to find a reason for this failure - I generated VCD traces for the litex simulation, analyzed them in gtkwave and here is what I found.

This is a part of disassembled `bios.bin`:
```
0000254c <litex_putc>:
   ...
   ...
    2562:	37ed                	jal	254c <litex_putc>
    2564:	40b2                	lw	ra,12(sp)
    2566:	8522                	mv	a0,s0
    2568:	4422                	lw	s0,8(sp)
    256a:	0141                	addi	sp,sp,16
    256c:	8082                	ret
```
During execution of this part of code a strange bug happens - at some point the CPU is executing `jal` instruction, but for some reason it saves 2566 as a return address instead of 2564. This results in omitting ` lw    ra,12(sp)`  instruction after we return from the function call. This `lw` instruction is responsible for restoring the return address of the caller function, but since it is not executed, the 2566 value is still left in `ra` register. Therefore, executing `ret` later on results in jumping to 2566 and we end up being stuck in some kind of "loop" (instructions 2566, 2568, 256a, 256c are being executed repeatadly).

The instructions here are 2-byte sized (compressed), but while executing the `jal` instruction, the CPU saves `pc+4` instead of `pc+2` as a return address, just as if the executed instruction was 4-byte sized  (not compressed). For this reason I decided to rerun the simulation, but this time with a binary, that doesn't contain compressed instructions (remove `c` from `march` in https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/blob/master/litex/soc/cores/cpu/cv32e41p/core.py#L32):

```

(reading some issues related to OpenHW group cores)

@panantoni01 Hum, strange...
Does it mean there would be a bug with compressed instructions on the 41P?
I haven't seen issues related to it in the openhwgroup repository... :neutral_face:

Thanks for the report and the detailed analysis.

I integrated a workaround/fix in cbac44ac3:
  cpu/cv32e41p: Avoid compressed codegen by default

The issue appears to come from firmware being built with RV32IMC by default. In the failing trace, a compressed `jal` stores `pc+4` instead of `pc+2` as the return address, which skips the caller return-address restore and leaves the BIOS stuck in a loop.

The CV32E41P `standard` variant now builds LiteX software as RV32IM, so GCC will not emit compressed instructions by default. I also kept the previous RV32IMC behavior available  explicitly through the new `imc` variant for anyone wanting to debug or validate the compressed path.

I added a focused regression test for the advertised GCC flags. Full `litex_sim --cpu-type=cv32e41p` boot still needs validation in an environment with `pythondata-cpu-cv32e41p`  installed.

Update: this issue appears to be in the CV32E41P CPU RTL, not in the LiteX wrapper.

The failing case is compressed code, specifically a `c.jal` path where the link address can become `pc+4` instead of `pc+2`. That writes the wrong return address, skips the caller's  `ra` restore, and then execution loops.

The root cause I found is that the RTL computes `is_compressed_o` in `cv32e41p_merged_decoder.sv`, but this signal is not declared as a decoder output port and is not connected in   `cv32e41p_id_stage.sv`. With permissive SystemVerilog handling, `id_stage_i.is_compressed` becomes an implicit undriven net, so the `IMMB_PCINCR` path can use the wrong increment.

The minimal CPU RTL patch that fixes the simulation is:

  ```diff
  diff --git a/rtl/cv32e41p_merged_decoder.sv b/rtl/cv32e41p_merged_decoder.sv
  @@
     input  logic [31:0] instr_rdata_i,
  +  output logic        is_compressed_o,

  diff --git a/rtl/cv32e41p_id_stage.sv b/rtl/cv32e41p_id_stage.sv
  @@
     logic is_clpx, is_subrot;
  +  logic is_compressed;
  @@
         .instr_rdata_i(instr),
  +      .is_compressed_o(is_compressed),
  ```

With this patch, cv32e41p/imc boots in LiteX simulation. However, since the upstream CV32E41P repository is archived, we cannot upstream the CPU RTL fix cleanly. So on the LiteX side  we will keep CV32E41P on the known-good standard RV32IM variant and avoid advertising an imc variant.
This is done with https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/commit/d86a229ea95b70a9c50d914adb28f03205abdd12 and cv32e41p is now also tested back in ci.

title: axi-lite CSR `.we` not obeying single-cycle interface spec
body:
According to:

https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/blob/937428b1fc3953bdc1726f292f4cb9bb163bf5cd/litex/soc/interconnect/csr.py#L98-L108

The `.re` and `.we` signals should pulse high for exactly one cycle. However, in practice, I am finding that on an `axi-lite` system, the `.we` signal stays high for longer than one cycle. 

I am using the following simple test bench to create CSRs that exercise the corner cases:

```python

            # test that caching is OFF for the I/O regions
            self.sim_coherence_w = CSRStorage(32, name= "wdata", description="Write values here to check cache coherence issues")
            self.sim_coherence_r = CSRStatus(32, name="rdata", description="Data readback derived from coherence_w")
            self.sim_coherence_inc = CSRStatus(32, name="rinc", description="Every time this is read, the base value is incremented by 3", reset=0)

            self.sync += [
                If(self.sim_coherence_inc.we,
                    self.sim_coherence_inc.status.eq(self.sim_coherence_inc.status + 3)
                ).Else(
                    self.sim_coherence_inc.status.eq(self.sim_coherence_inc.status)
                )
            ]
            self.comb += [
                self.sim_coherence_r.status.eq(self.sim_coherence_w.storage + 5)
            ]
```

This is connected to a system that uses an axi-lite bus via a crossbar framework that uses axi, so the overall connectivity is CPU (axi4) -> crossbar (axi4) -> AXI2Axilite -> Axilite2Simple -> CSR banks.

Basically, the test bench will "add 3" to `rinc` every time it is read, so successive reads should generate a series of numbers like 0, 3, 6, 9, ...

This is what I'm seeing in practice:

![image](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1168375/205859545-081364de-9c83-4506-aa75-c05043181d72.png)

The `.we` signal stays selected for much more than one cycle, so the register increments more than it should.

The `.we` signal seems this is derived from this code:

https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/blob/937428b1fc3953bdc1726f292f4cb9bb163bf5cd/litex/soc/interconnect/csr_bus.py#L183-L198

The `sel` comes from just checking that the address matches, and is then applied with the `If(sel, Case(...))` in the final `sync` section at the bottom. Thus it's assumed that the address provided on the bus should be valid for exactly one cycle to create a one-cycle wide `.we` pulse.

However, the address is applied for multiple cycles. The AXI->Axilite and back again conversion can't complete in a single cycle, so the address is asserted for multiple cycles as the whole round-trip completes.

I'm guessing this bug may not have been noticed because not many systems trigger errors if a CSR is read from multiple times. In practice I don't have any blocks that break if this spec is violated, but, I would really like the axi-lite CSR implementation to behave spec-identical to the wishbone stuff, it would make me sleep better at night.

That being said, I am running into myriad issues trying to rework the system to obey this discipline. There are issues both in the Axi2Axilite converter, and also in the CSR interface itself. The Axi2Axilite converter is issuing two cycles for every one AXI request, and the CSR interface behavior doesn't match what's expected of AXI due to a mismatch in cycle delays, so the fix isn't simple.

I'll open a PR to address this issue but all my code also depends on PR #1506 being accepted, since I can't run simulations without it.

The problem lays in, amongst others, in the file `litex/build/yosys_wrapper.py`. Here the command is created and the string is terminated by a new-line character, i.e.:
```
base_cmd = f"yosys -l {self._build_name}.rpt {self._build_name}.ys\n"
```

In `litex/build/yosys_nextpnr_toolchain.py` the fail-statement is added using string concatenation, so that will end up on the next line. This only affects Windows, because for Linux does not use `fail_stmt` at this moment.

To solve this issue, there are two possible solutions:

1.  Not terminating the commands with `\n`, but leave that to the `build_script` function. This means all functions for commands have to be checked (not only the yosys+nextpnr-ecp5 toolchain I use.
2.  In the `build_script` command use `.rstrip` to strip all white-space (including newlines) from the command. 

I would recommend to go for the second option. In that case the function would look like this:
```python
...
        # yosys call
        script_contents += f"{self._yosys.get_yosys_call('script').rstrip()} {fail_stmt\n"
        # nextpnr call
        script_contents += f"{self._nextpnr.get_call('script').rstrip()} {fail_stmt}\n"
...
```

The wrappers now  return command strings without trailing newlines and the build script generation adds the failure handler/newline in one place.

When I try to compile software for a NaxRiscv SoC using a 32-bits version of the RISC-V toolchain, it fails as the toolchain cannot be detected.

I believe that this issue does not depend on my setup but originates from line 141 in NaxRiscv's ```core.py``` file :

Related issue:
Meson build doesn't seem to work with the new RISC-V GCC tool chain.
```
../../../pythondata-software-picolibc/pythondata_software_picolibc/data/meson.build:35:0: ERROR: Value "c18" (of type "string") for combo option "C language standard to use" is not one of the choices. Possible choices are (as string): "none", "c89", "c99", "c11", "gnu89", "gnu99", "gnu11".
```
Do I have the wrong one on the path?

> Tools don't like the new Meson Release Dec 23.

https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litex/blob/e8322587a06f2f3e82443cc6422ba230b11c195a/litex/soc/integration/builder.py#L256-L266

This seems like a pretty odd check to me. It's checking to see if the major version is older than 0, OR if the minor version is older than 59.

Checking the major version doesn't even make *sense*, the minimum requirement here is "0".

Anyway, this check is definitely not a real version comparison. It should use a version tuple instead:

```python
if tuple(int(i) for i in meson_version[:3]) < (0, 59, 0):
         msg = f"Meson version too old. Found ......."
```

Because it's not an either-or.

You could also do this:
```meson
from packaging.version import Version

meson_version = Version(subprocess.check_output(["meson", "-v"]).decode("utf-8"))

if meson_version < Version('0.59.0'):
    msg = f"Meson version too old. Found ......."
```

That does require the https://pypi.org/project/packaging/ module, which is reasonably common at least. It also guarantees proper "version specifiers" support.
The new `apt install riscv64-linux-gnu-gcc` default to gcc 7.5 which causes the second meson error listed above.
Google colab uses Ubuntu 18 and therefore only installs the riscv64 gcc 7.5.  I had to manually install the newer RISCV binaries.
